chapter_theme: A must elephant charges Gunamalai's palanquin; her bearers flee and her companion offers to die with her, and Civakan, judging death better than standing by, draws the beast on himself, escapes its trunk and drives it off, a deed the narrator measures by Krishna's. Taken home withered, Gunamalai turns from her kin like one who knows her births and, alone with her companions, confesses her love-sickness in images of Kama's archery, the sacrificial fire and the want of those who did no penance.

cast.role: the hero, who saves Gunamalai from the elephant
a merchant's daughter, Suramanjari's rival in the powder contest, whom Civakan saves and marries
Gunamalai's companion, left with her before the elephant
Gunamalai's mother, wife of a great merchant
Gunamalai's loving kin, who take her home
the young men who bear Gunamalai's palanquin and flee
the must elephant that charges Gunamalai's palanquin

974.reading: The elephant, streaming must like a falling cascade and with blood on its tusks, breaks loose, and the people who had filled every quarter vanish from sight like the many stars that hide before the sun.
974.event: The must elephant runs amok and the crowds scatter out of sight.

975.reading: As the great tusker rushes on her as the hearts of lustful men rush on a dark-eyed woman, the bearers drop the palanquin and run, and the girl's companion, crying out whether there are no men, raises her joined hands above her head and bows before the elephant.
975.event: The bearers abandon Gunamalai's palanquin, and her companion bows to the elephant and calls for help.
975.nuance: The simile of line 1 sets the elephant's charge beside men's desire for the woman, so that the danger and the courtship to come are drawn from one figure.

976.reading: The companion resolves: let it kill me together with her, or let some man appear in time to save her dear life; if not, whatever comes after my eyes have closed may come; and she stands trembling like lightning, looking at the beast.
976.event: Gunamalai's companion resolves to die with her unless a rescuer comes.
976.nuance: The thought (lines 1-3) is the companion's, closed by என்றெண்ணி; whether the one who stands trembling in line 4, likened to a flower-laden golden creeper, is the companion or Gunamalai herself the verse does not settle.

977.reading: Civakan, his hair bound up with a gold cord tipped with gems at both ends and wreathed with a garland, his ear-drops swinging and his loyal companions around him, is passing by when he sees the girl's peril.
977.event: Civakan, passing with his companions, sees the danger to the girl.

978.reading: Seeing a woman's life in danger, the noble one reckons death better than living on; at once he winds up his flower garland, pushes up his golden bracelet, binds his cloth with his belt, curses the elephant and runs at it shouting.
978.event: Civakan girds himself and runs at the elephant.

claims.claim: for a noble man, death is better than living on while a woman's life is in danger

978.nuance: வாழ்வின் சாதல் எண்ணினன் is a judgment the narrator gives the hero at the moment of choice, before any thought of who the woman is: the rescue is first a matter of honour, and love comes after.

979.reading: The young man leaps like lightning falling on a hill and strikes the forehead of the mighty elephant with a clap of his arms, while his round pearls, chain, garland and hair fly and the open flowers of his wreath scatter.
979.event: Civakan leaps at the elephant and strikes its forehead.

980.reading: Just as the must elephant bends to crush the girl, he springs at it like Garuda upon a hooded cobra, like a lion leaping on the brow of the western mountain, and roars like thunder so that the beast's rage turns on him.
980.event: Civakan springs at the elephant as it stoops over Gunamalai, drawing its fury to himself.
980.nuance: The roar has a purpose the verse states: குப்புற்று ... உடல்சினங் கடவ, he turns the elephant's anger from the girl to himself.

981.reading: The elephant roars like Death, beats at him between its tusks with its trunk, shrieks like the wind and pours must in fury; the strong youth, unafraid as it runs at him, tells those near to take the bangled girl and get her to safety.
981.event: As the elephant turns on him, Civakan orders the girl carried away to safety.

982.reading: As the great serpent that climbs to seize the moon spreads its hood and runs at the sun, the fighting elephant leaves the girl and seizes in its trunk the man whose shoulders were made for those who have no refuge.
982.event: The elephant leaves Gunamalai and seizes Civakan in its trunk.
982.nuance: The eclipse simile makes Civakan the sun (பருதி) and the elephant the serpent of eclipse; பெற்றார்க்கு அதியமை தோளினான் praises him as a refuge in the very line in which he is caught.

983.reading: The moment it seizes him he slips free quick as lightning from a rain cloud, dives between its pearl-tipped tusks, folds himself small beneath its feet like the clay ball an expert plays, and the anklet-wearing hero, keeping out of its reach there, drives it far away.
983.event: Civakan wriggles free, dodges between the tusks and under the feet, and drives the elephant off.
983.nuance: கரந்துசே ணகற்றினான் can be read as his hiding and driving the beast far off or as his vanishing far away himself; the next verse, in which the elephant withdraws, favours the first.

984.reading: The elephant was like the tusker that once ran to kill the gem-coloured lord of the wide waters, and Civakan was like that lord; and the elephant dripping triple must, as if a god were in it, gave way.
984.event: The elephant gives way before Civakan.
984.nuance: The simile is the story of Krishna and the elephant sent against him, told in one line without naming either; a Jain epic uses the Vaishnava deed as a measure of its hero without comment. தெய்வம்போல் may go with Civakan (godlike, he stood) or with the elephant (as if possessed); the line division favours the elephant.

985.reading: Having beaten the one-trunked, two-tusked, triple-must elephant, tall as a fair hill, for the young girl, Civakan of the honey-scented garland and pearl-bright chest goes alone to the pleasure garden while his five hundred and four companions crowd round praising his feet.
985.event: Civakan, victorious, goes to the garden while his companions praise him.
985.nuance: ஐஞ்ஞாற்று நால்வர் reads as five hundred and four; the verse sets their praise beside தனியே போய், so 'alone' must mean apart from the girl and her people, not without his friends. The verse is in a longer metre than its neighbours.

986.reading: Her own people, whose love never slackens, take away the golden creeper whose distress the man of shoulders thick as a jewelled post had removed, telling her not to grieve.
986.event: Gunamalai's kin take her home and comfort her.

987.reading: The mother of the spear-eyed girl, beloved wife of the man who is a bull among the merchants with hands that give out great wealth from the roaring sea, sees her daughter wilted like a crushed garland and speaks.
987.event: Gunamalai's mother sees her wilted and speaks.

988.reading: 'What has come on my girl today, that she has withered and lost her golden colour like a hand-made garland thrust into a high ghee-fed flame?' she asks; and those who knew kept from telling, for wanting to come through safe.
988.event: The mother asks what has withered her daughter; the companions keep silent.
988.nuance: The verse turns from the mother's question (lines 1-3) to the silence of those who know: the companions hide the danger, and with it the cause of her withering, out of fear for themselves.

989.reading: Calling 'come', the mother wipes the tears from her daughter's bright eyes and embraces her, whose hair is full of mullai garlands drunk by bees and whose slender waist bends.
989.event: The mother calls her daughter to her, wipes her tears and embraces her.

990.reading: With the companions who never let go of her hand, the mother searches it out by her own understanding and finds that the girl's grief came upon her at the festive gathering.
990.event: The mother, questioning the companions, learns where the trouble began.
990.nuance: Line 1 (கடம்பு சூடிய கன்னி மாலைபேற்) is hard to construe; it may tie the gathering to a rite of the kadambu-wearing god, and the text may be corrupt (மாலைபெற்).

991.reading: They take off her heavy worked ornaments and put light ones on her body, set a soft garland on her and smear saffron over the creeper-like girl.
991.event: The women change Gunamalai's heavy jewels for light ones and anoint her.

992.reading: Her green parrot calls to the girl, 'go and fetch our sister who brings nectar in a golden cup', and our girl like a golden creeper goes.
992.event: Gunamalai's pet parrot calls out, and she goes.
992.nuance: Who is fetched and where the girl goes are not clear: the parrot's words may ask for its keeper, or may be a call the girl, lost in thought, answers by walking away. The verse ends in the voice of her own household (எம் பாவை).

993.reading: The girl whose red-lined eyes have stolen the power of the fat-smeared spear spurns all the talk of her kin, like those who have come to know their births, and wants nothing at all.
993.event: Gunamalai turns from her family's talk and from everything else.

claims.claim: those who have come to know their births turn away from the talk of kin and desire nothing

993.nuance: பிறப்பு உணர்ந்தவர் may mean those who recall their former births, the knowledge that in the epic's world turns a person to renunciation; the narrator lends the love-struck girl the renouncer's withdrawal, though her wanting nothing is wanting one man.

994.reading: Finding a moment apart from her people, the girl like a creeper in a garland tells of her love for the youth, who is like the lord who appeared on the lotus to the gods' delight.
994.event: Away from her kin, Gunamalai speaks of her love for Civakan.
994.nuance: The lord born on the lotus to the gods' desire, called குமரன், reads as Murugan of the reed pool; the verse names Civakan only by the likeness.

995.reading: Gunamalai says that the cruel five-arrowed one practises his archery on her, making the time of union his school's hall, the space between her breasts his heap of target earth, and her life his mark.
995.nuance: Kama is an archer in training and she the butt: the conceit turns her pain into his practice, so that it will go on.

996.reading: 'Since even the earth could not bear it, my heart burns like the fire of a sacrifice: bring me quickly the man of the garlanded chest, Civaka Sami, who is Kama himself, ladies.'
996.nuance: The name சீவக சாமி, by which the invocation calls the hero, is here in the mouth of a girl who wants him as a lover.

997.reading: 'I speak with my hands and hear with my eyes; with a mind crowded with thought I have become a mute; like the small folk who did no penance, is there any door by which I can be saved?'

claims.claim: those who have done no penance have no way to reach what they long for

997.nuance: Speaking by hand and hearing by eye describes her silence before others: she cannot say her love aloud. The simile measures a lover's want by the want of those without the merit of past tapas.

links.note: The patikam gives the episode one line, the victorious elephant that terrified Gunamalai, beaten on the same day Civakan gave nectar to the dying dog; 974-985 tell it as a scene in which the bearers flee, the companion offers to die, and Civakan chooses death over life before he knows who the girl is.
links.teaches: The patikam's pairing of the dog and the elephant on one day is borne out by the scene's terms: both deeds are mercy to a life in danger, not courtship, and the love follows only afterwards.

links.note: Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak that will not live without its hair; 978 has Civakan reckon death better than life when a stranger woman's life is in danger.
links.teaches: The epic moves the Kural's honour-death from guarding one's own standing to rescuing another, so that honour is measured by whose danger a man will not stand by and watch.

gains.a: a rule that names the choice Civakan makes in a single line as a settled standard of honour, not a hero's impulse
gains.b: a case where the life given up for honour is risked to save someone else, which the couplet's self-regarding image of the yak leaves out

links.note: In Akananuru 18 the friend tells the lover that if her friend suffers harm for a single day she will not live after; in 976 Gunamalai's companion, facing the elephant, resolves that it should kill her together with her mistress.
links.teaches: The akam friend's stock claim that her life hangs on the heroine's is put to the test in the epic by a real beast, and the companion keeps it, so the convention is shown as a loyalty that can be acted on.

gains.a: the akam convention behind the companion's resolve, which makes her offer a known role rather than a passing panic
gains.b: an enacted instance of the friend's pledge, which the poem only states as a warning to the lover

links.note: In Kalittokai 103 a herdsman wrenching a charging bull by the ear is likened to Mayon tearing the horse's jaw, and the herd girls will embrace only one who falls between the killer bull's horns; in 984 Civakan facing the elephant is likened to the gem-coloured lord facing the elephant sent to kill him, and Gunamalai's love follows.
links.teaches: Both poems make the man who masters a charging beast a Krishna figure whom a girl then loves, but the herders' bull-catch is a set contest whose price the community names, while the epic's rescue is unplanned and the girl chooses for herself.

gains.a: the older pattern of beast-taming as a bride-winning feat under a Krishna simile, which explains why the elephant fight leads straight into Gunamalai's love
gains.b: a later merchant-city version of the pattern in which the danger falls on the girl and the feat is a rescue, not a sport

links.note: Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go silently, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest-tree; 993 says Gunamalai spurns her kin's talk like those who know their births.
links.teaches: The epic borrows the renouncer's detachment from kin, which the Naladiyar grounds in kin's passing, to picture a girl whose turning from family is love for one man, so the same outward withdrawal is shown to have opposite causes.

gains.a: the reasoning about kin as passing visitors that the simile's 'those who know their births' assumes but does not state
gains.b: a sign that the quatrain's lesson had become a known figure of speech, usable even of a lover's absorption

links.note: Kural 270 says the have-nots are many because few do penance; 997 has Gunamalai ask whether, like the small folk who did no penance, she has any door to escape her longing.
links.teaches: The couplet's explanation of want by the lack of past tapas is taken up by a lover as an account of why the man she wants is out of reach, showing the doctrine at work in ordinary speech about desire.

gains.a: the doctrinal sense of her simile: that what one lacks is owed to penance not done, which turns her cry into a judgment on her own merit
gains.b: a reading of the couplet's unspecified 'those who lack' as covering the lover's lack, which the couplet leaves open

source_issues: Verses 974, 975, 976, 979, 980, 981, 983 and 985 were printed in eight half-lines and have been joined into four (FLAG repaired).
Verse 975 line 4 prints றோருங்குகை, which the sense requires as றொருங்கு கை (joining both hands); a misdivision or misprint.
Verse 978 line 4 prints ஆர்ததுமே, probably ஆர்த்து மேல் (shouting, upon it); a dropped letter.
Verse 990 line 1 prints மாலைபேற், probably மாலைபெற்; the line is hard to construe either way.
Verse 985 is in a longer metre than the verses around it and gives the number of Civakan's companions as ஐஞ்ஞாற்று நால்வர் (five hundred and four).
